This study examines the discretization of an optimal stochastic control problem involving the parabolic differential equations, with both control variables included in diffusion. Through this study, convergence for this problem is established, even in situations where the input values contain errors; additionally, a Monte Carlo technique is proposed.

This study analyzes in-depth the large-scale anisotropies of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (exceeding 4 EeV) recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory, specifically examining the energy intervals of 4–8 EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV. While retaining the earlier finding of the notable right ascension-dependent dipolar modulation observed at energies beyond 8 EeV, we perform a more rigorous examination of the highest energy bin by subdividing it into three distinct ranges. Our analysis reveals that the dipole amplitude systematically increases with energy for sources above 4 EeV, following a power law characterized by an index of $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$ over this high-energy span, while maintaining consistency in the dipole directions with predicted sources from an extragalactic distribution across the studied spectrum. We also assessed quadrupolar anisotropy components, finding them to lack statistical significance, of the results are contextualized against various models regarding the cosmic source distributions and ultra-high-energy source and cosmic structure. We further evaluate these findings within the framework of theoretical predictions describing ultra-high-energy source distributions and cosmic-ray magnetic fields.

This study examines the challenges of managing discrepancies in relational tables containing missing values (nulls) alongside functional dependencies (FDs). While the conventional wisdom holds that table instances must adhere strictly to all imposed FDs, it is crucial to develop methodologies addressing how instances that violate some dependencies can be managed concerning nulls, specifically by developing methods for defining and assessing consistency with respect to FDs and the associated concept of table integrity checks. Furthermore, several applications highlight the relevance of this work in areas such as data cleaning, machine learning, and knowledge graphs. To support these activities, we have developed a system tool called nullREPLACE. This database utility enables the handling, verification, and consistency of relational tables with nulls by enforcing user-defined functional dependencies, accepting such tables even if they currently exhibit inconsistencies. Regarding theoretical underpinnings, we introduce a specific interpretation regarding table consistency that assumes functional determinism extends also to targets with missing entries, despite the source attributes being missing values. Additionally, we define a mechanism for representing missing data as an unknown functional relation characterized by a specific integrity constraint property termed "closed consistency." Within this framework, we investigate the matter of identifying if such a consistency can be established when a table relates to a particular functional dependency. To support these investigations, we define a class of consistent assignments for table rows with respect to any given FD, based on a logic of "partially ordered functions" that orders all potential relationships between particular source attributes and unknown targets where missing data exists,

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation technique that encodes points and the relative poses between an object and specific targets—like robotic grippers or hanging racks—utilizing category-level features. Leveraged in object manipulation, this approach allows a learned task, demonstrated by experts on one instance within a category, to be replicated on unseen instances of that same category. The desired pose is determined through an optimization process seeking a pose descriptor that aligns with those captured in the desired task state. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our optimization-based reconstruction, we first highlight how desired poses can be accurately learned from background-rich, multi-object scenes containing unseen items. Furthermore, we show the scalability of this method for tasks involving numerous distinct objects. Crucially, we establish SE(3)-equivariance within the descriptor learning framework, ensuring robust and robust task execution under rigid transformations of the scene. Extensive experiments validate the robustness of our proposed approach against occlusions, lighting variations, and, most notably, unseen test objects.

In various contemporary challenges in statistical mechanics and machine learning, there is a prevalent interest in demonstrating that first-order optimization schemes on non-convex loss surfaces eventually reach regions within the parameter space where the risk function becomes locally convex. We introduce an asymptotic comparison criterion termed the Sudakov-Fernique post-AMP inequality; within a specific framework of problems involving GOE matrices, this criterion enables the investigation of optimization landscape properties adjacent to iterates generated by approximate message passing (AMP). To illustrate its application, we present an asymptotic analysis of the cycle structure within the solution set for GOE spin glass system, as initially examined by Approximate Message Passing iterations.

Although the use of stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optics appears simple, attaining 0.01 precision for vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) has remained elusive. Achieving this target relies on wide-field photometry spanning diverse altitudes, which speeds up VAOD derivation without needing the system's absolute calibration, while simultaneously delivering that calibration incidentally. This study details the setup and one year of results for the MASTER-UV stellar network at Roboteck, Israel, achieving a precision of approximately 0.015 VAOD, or 1.3 times the signal noise at the system's center. The calibration of the photometric system was achieved via an initial campaign using long-exposure images against bright stars, followed by one year utilizing the network's inherent linearity; this method is especially valuable for ground-based systems. Additionally, optimizing exposure intervals and systematic scheduling patterns significantly enhances both the frequency of observations (cadence) and overall observational accuracy.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to solve general Graphical Lasso issues. The graphical Lasso method, a framework introduced by Dempster in a classic work, estimates the inverse covariance matrix and thereby reveals the concentration graph of the data. Building on this foundation, GGLasso extends the approach through several key features. It supports various penalization schemes, including group Lasso and graph-structured penalties. Furthermore, the system facilitates the integration of prior knowledge about the graph via multiple construction methods such as hierarchical clustering. Additionally, GGLasso offers a suite of post-selection inference tools to determine precise p-values for edge significance within the resulting graph. Finally, we evaluate GGLasso against leading alternatives for inverse covariance discovery in various experimental settings. This demonstrates the package's efficiency and ease regarding parameter tuning and computational speed.

This study assesses and compares numerous numerical techniques designed to handle the stochastic differential equations arising in molecular dynamics, which combine drift, deterministic forces, and Brownian noise. Leveraging recent findings on Baker-Campbell-Hauodroff (Hottau-Bauer-Haassdorff/HB) expansions, we examine how step size introduces biases into configurational averaging to enhance sampling precision. We find that for harmonic oscillators—critical for modeling biomolecule bond stretching—select schemes yield exact configurational averages, while an identified optimal approach minimizes bias for general systems. After detailing our rigorous benchmarking framework, we apply it to simulate protein folding, demonstrating a clear superior performance using our recommended method over conventional alternatives.

We introduce a novel method for computing a specific type of eigenvector centrality applicable to multilayer networks subject to cross-layer constraints on node significance. These networks consist of multiple layers—each an edge-weighted and potentially directed graph sharing the same set of nodes—but contain no inter-layer connections. Similar to classic eigenvector centrality, a node's importance within a layer depends on the weighted relevance of its neighbors within that same layer. However, unlike the standard model, we allow a node's importance in one layer to be constrained by its weights in other layers. To address these multi-level constraints, we reformulate the problem as a matrix spiral iteration and solve it through a generalized power method. We also extend this framework to multilayer networks that do share inter-layer connections.

We have recently established a new R-Poincar\[c\]e model (without supersymmetry) that remains invariant under full R-Poincar\[c\]e transformations, even when the deformation parameter is finite. Within this framework, the anti-Lie algebra generated by constant-coefficient generators, when restricted to generators lacking deformation, corresponds to the de Sitter (dS) spacetime. Furthermore, through a suitable transformation of the translation generators, the algebra reorganizes into anti-Lie so(3,2), implying that the underlying geometric space is de Sitter. Consequently, our model aligns spacetime geometry with de Sitter curvature while preserving its distinct algebraic properties. Concluding from this duality, we propose labeling the space R-Poincar\[c\]e and designating the governing algebra the dS-P\[c\]Oincare algebra.

This study investigates sphere entry into water across a range of velocities, with particular focus on the resulting impact regimes. The primary aim is to define the boundaries between the air cushioning and surface tension sealing modes. A novel theoretical framework addressing the surface seal condition is introduced; this extends previous theories by incorporating effects of sphere curvature and curvature forces. Validated against both existing literature data and extensive new experimental campaigns, this current model, when combined with the air cushion model, allows for the accurate prediction of regime transitions. These findings include the critical Froude and Weber numbers marking the shift between air cushioning and surface sealing behaviors, as well as specific details on oscillation frequencies and initial impact velocities within the surface seal category. Additional experimental evidence for low-velocity regimes is also provided, including those dominated by gravity and those where surface wetting plays a decisive role.

A persistent conjecture posits that global symmetries cannot exist within quantum gravity. By examining extensive families of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, the possible generalized global symmetries and mechanisms to avoid them are investigated. Essential components in these theories are generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear couplings among axion fields and terms topological quadratic in gauge curvatures, thereby disrupting many global symmetries. Any resulting residual symmetries can also be broken if certain charged states exist. We demonstrate, however, that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect; the implication is that a lattice of infinitely charged states forms. Furthermore, it is established that this lattice originates from the monodromy transformation, defined at the boundary of the moduli space near which these theories are formulated.

We investigate the spectral properties of a low-symmetry 2D electronic lattice: a herringbone system within a non-symmorphic wallpaper group defined by orthogonal glide symmetries along two sets of directions. Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding framework incorporating horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two inequivalent Dirac cones located along a specific path in the first Brillouin zone (FBZ), which can be adjusted through various Hamiltonian perturbations. Initially, introducing distinct onsite potentials breaks the underlying lattice symmetries, causing the annihilation of Dirac points into nodal lines or semi-Dirac points on the same FBZ directions. Further symmetry breaking via hopping term dimerization triggers the reorganization of Dirac points into trajectories tracing out quasi-hyperbolic lines across the FBZ. Additionally, we outline a real-space realization by depositing CO atoms atop a Cu(111) crystal surface.

We produce Single-Photon Catalyzed Coherent States (SPCCSs) utilizing quantum optical methods that depend either on beam splitters (BS) or parametric amplifiers (PA). To obtain these states, a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state at two input ports undergo interaction with the device; simultaneously, detecting one photon in the second output port yields an SPCCS in the opposite ouput channel. Differences in the success probabilities associated with detection and normalization are highlighted between BS and PA protocols. Furthermore, we provide analytical proofs demonstrating that despite differing generation mechanisms via BS and PA, the final resulting quantum states are mathematically identical after the electron-photon number distribution of each state is evaluated by examining both the particle structure and the state's $W$-representation.

The application of bivectors within General Relativity and the Newman-Penrose formalism is essential for formulating the exact solutions of Einstein's field equations. This paper serves as a guided introduction to the core principles and concepts of gravitational bivectors. It highlights their utility in deriving multiple exact Einstein solutions and provides the specific expressions for bivectors under a supergravity solution known as the C-metric.

Delineating esophageal tumors in CT scans presents a dual challenge for manual and automatic segmentation: the low tissue contrast near these lesions and the high inter-delineation effort. To address this, the authors introduced a fully automated method beginning with a registration framework utilizing two dilated sub-networks to estimate a tumor prior from a reference to a target image. This prior helps contour both well- and poorly visible lesions equally. Subsequently, vertex-aligned contours are refined via an active contour algorithm guided by an intensity-driven objective, distance-driven initialization, and the previously estimated prior. Validation using a cohort of 138 pairs of contaminated and clean scans demonstrated that the method effectively segments visible lesions (median DSC of 0.911) as effectively as it handles obscured tumors (median DSC 0.831), with performance largely influenced by whether the lesion appears clearly or is masked in the images.

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages for both spoken and written communication, multilingualism frequently manifests through code-switching or code-mixing within individual sentences. This work reviews existing natural language processing (NLP) literature regarding its limitations and obstacles when addressing five critical social impact areas: crisis response, healthcare support, political engagement, anti-disinformation strategies, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual communities. Furthermore, we introduce prospective datasets, models, and utilities poised to propel multilingual NLP research toward broader societal benefits. Utilizing English-Hindi mixing as a case study allows for representative inferences applicable to other languages pairs.

Automatic image description models are typically built and assessed on crowd-sourced human references, with the top-performing system selected by measuring similarity against these references using metrics such as BLEU, CIDER, or METEOR. Consequently, since both system performance and evaluation accuracy hinge on these descriptions, ensuring their high quality and safety has become critical—particularly given that description datasets contain biases and unsafe material like profanity or controversial topics inherited from web sources such as MS-COCO Descriptions. In this paper, we introduce a family of techniques designed to detect and remove unsafe image-text pairs from description datasets. We begin by applying a co-occurrence filter, utilizing the visual similarity between query and target images to determine if a specific description poses a security risk. We enhance this base approach with two advanced methods: a difficulty estimator and a specificity estimator, refining the identification process. Evaluation results indicate that this pipeline effectively identifies inappropriate pairs in the crowdsource data, yielding cleaner datasets. Furthermore, neural models trained exclusively on this purified version significantly lowered their unpredictability scores relative to standard reference descriptions while simultaneously maintaining equivalent levels of captioning accuracy and safety.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) exhibit favorable physical and chemical traits, including strong antireflective capabilities and high dielectric constants. In addition, recent studies suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles could enhance biological efficacy in cancer hadron therapy, and first-principles simulations offer a robust method for exploring their electronic structures. However, the multicomponent nature of the Ta-O system poses significant challenges for standard density functional theory (DFT) calculations using localized basis sets like those in VASP. To address this, we conducted an extensive benchmarking study of the J-parameter-included U correction within QMC and highly accurate MP2 methodologies, specifically targeting key DFT predictions such as band gaps, absorption coefficients, and hydrostatic equation of state parameters. Furthermore, we performed targeted QMC and MP2 calculations on selected results to validate the effectiveness of our refined CVPSSS/PBE-DHMQCC approach equipped with numerical points meshes. Ultimately, this precise quantum Monte Carlo strategy emerges as an ideal framework for predicting the dosimetry and depth-distribution profiles essential for medical applications involving tantalum oxides.

Previous studies mostly attibuted the rapid circulation of news, even misinformation, to characteristics within news items or media platforms and user behaviors. Our research offers a novel city-level analysis demonstrating that a significant factor is the geographic distribution of users and specific traits, particularly conscientiousness. Our findings indicate that one reason for the pandemic-era prevalence of fake news was likely the high levels of this personality trait among those sharing it. Increased fake news activity occurred in states ranked higher for conscientiousness during periods when actual news volume decreased elsewhere. We observe that while raw sharing rates were not uniformly elevated across all locations city-wide, the contextual influence of fake news sharing rose uniquely with conscientiousness (after controlling for other dimensions). At the individual level, we found that fake news sharing by more conscientious users was significantly predicted by higher frequencies of other fake news shares from peers with similar characteristics. Finally, we offer a theoretical rationale suggesting why high conscientiousness might paradoxically lead to fake news dissemination in this specific context.

Conversational interfaces, which utilize natural language interfaces to automate interaction processes and enhance user experience, have gained significant momentum in recent technology. These systems, encompassing both research and commercial applications, include virtual assistants and chatbots designed to manage complex dialogue tasks autonomously. However, the dependency on vast annotated datasets for model training poses a substantial barrier to development, particularly in niche domains such as legal services. To address this challenge, our work introduces a document-centric evaluation framework using a four-year corpus of Supreme Court opinions from the IBM Supreme Court Database (SCDB). This initiative yields a publicly available version containing 388,318 individual claims from across the United States legal system, each manually labeled with its corresponding Black's Law Dictionary term. By focusing on sentence segment classification rather than full sentence analysis, this project offers a cost-effective method for data annotation and provides an efficient avenue for sharing knowledge derived from the rich, curated dataset.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant interest from researchers for its potential to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems. Nevertheless, existing single- or dual-target CDR techniques frequently face limitations, including the requirement that one domain be abundant in data, a requirement that seems unrealistic in many real-world multi-domain scenarios. Addressing these challenges, we introduce MSDCR, a Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation framework. MSDCR simultaneously targets specific items in one sparse domain and the overall domain in another sparse context, without assuming data richness in either domain. We achieve this by developing a novel source-of-trust mechanism, a filtering process to ensure high quality, and a mutual learning approach tailored specifically to learning from trust within both domains. Our extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that MSDCR significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods.

Numerous convex optimization tasks can be framed as minimizing an objective function of linear operators over specific exotic cones. These cones include symmetric nonnegative matrices, the pseudocone associated with the sum-of-mixed-products form, and the Lorentz cone derived from the partial ordered structure of the bigger nonnegative matrix conex. In each instance, we show how solving the corresponding finite-size convex problem as a second-order cone program (SOCP) yields more efficient solutions compared to standard approaches, because the required number of scalars grows only as the square root of the size parameter rather than the size itself. Consequently, these methods offer substantial computational advantages for infinite collection of problems encompassing convex basing, positive matrix deconvolution, and the positive matrix deconvolution.

Rapidly advancing automated quality control (AQC) systems serve as a vital component of clinical workflows within MRI investigations, yet a key obstacle to their widespread adoption lies in the scarcity of publicly available datasets for performance verification. To overcome this limitation, this project evaluates a range of current AQC methodologies on an MRI dataset depicting patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls. To ensure the study maintains clinical relevance and authenticity, all data was intentionally distorted through various acquisition inconsistencies, such as severe motion artifacts and intentional erasures. Furthermore, the feasibility of deploying these systems as self-sustaining models was assessed by examining the incorporation of content-aware transformations for mutual structural normalization and retraining algorithms without utilizing quality labels during acquisition. Evaluations were conducted using both subjective human assessment and objective metrics, yielding highly consistent outcomes. The study demonstrates that effective automation can be achieved through combined approaches of deep learning and conventional techniques, even amidst significant image degradation, confirming that prior normalization does need to happen, and that adaptive transformations substantially enhance performance. Moreover, the study observes that while quality assessment metrics exhibit diverse behaviors, a threshold-based decision rule using a weighted combination of such metrics emerges as a particularly viable strategy. Since this algorithm surpasses the performance of independently tested single methods, the results establish a comparative benchmark that validates the chosen approach against the best-performing individual systems.

This paper examines the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power system stability during disruptions. To capture the decentralized interactions within transportation and energy domains, we introduce a Network-based Multi-Agent Optimization (N-MAO) framework formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming problem. Specifically, this study focuses on the joint decision process for vehicle-matching pairs and generation-matching pairs, aiming to maximize overall social value. A key contribution is the Resilience-Based Unit Commitment (RBUC) model, which determines the commitment status of generators to address potential outages. Furthermore, two multi-agent optimization subproblems are addressed non-heuristically: a Decentralized Network Flow Model for efficient vehicle scheduling routes and cost-effective charging plans, and a Decentralized Network Expansion Model, also of low cost, intended to optimize the placement of vehicle matching pairs and generation-matching pairs with decentralized decision-making. These models are integrated into a comprehensive R-MAO framework characterized by multiple tiers and time scales, ensuring robustness and efficiency. Computational experiments validate this proposed methodology's effectiveness and feasibility.

Through analytical characterisation of bifurction properties and numerical analysis, the study illustrates how the resulting model demonstrates a complex recurrence consistent with a strange attractor.

We examine predictions within the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model that modifies the gauge group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$. This reformulation eliminates bare charged vector bosons, requiring charge to arise from spontaneous symmetry breaking via a mechanism analogous to neutral meson mixing. Consequently, the model forecasts a rich physical spectrum, specifically including charged composite states with masses in the multi-TeV range, as well as neutral composite scalars (pseudo-Goldstone states) with masses near 1 TeV. Experimental constraints from LHC operations at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ and $13$ Ge provide significant guidance on these parameters; the compiled combined limits are notably lower than previously anticipated theoretical expectations or direct measurements. Furthermore, the model's predicted tri-generation of fermions, inferred directly from the expanded gauge symmetry, offers an inherent advantage in addressing current anomalies regarding scalar lepton production.

We examine the commutation laws within this extended standard framework for group $G_n$ (likely a classical subgroup of $S_n$) and establish their connection to the Hecke algebra of type $A$. Importantly, we define a modified OOG for the special groups of type $S_k$ and type $S_n$ to ensure defined commutation within composite structures $G_k \times G_n$.

Developing robust, high-performance interfaces between silicon telecom photons and spins will significantly advance global quantum networks. T radiation damage centres in silicon are a promising candidate for such interfaces, offering long lifetimes for both nuclear and electron spins alongside an optically distinct, narrow O-band transition centered near 1326 nm. While these centres have previously been restricted to bulk silicon ensemble studies, this work demonstrates their reliable formation within the 220 nm device layers of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates using ion implantation and thermal annealing to achieve high concentrations. Furthermore, we establish a methodology leveraging spin-selective optical transitions to assess intrinsic spectral diffusi'on characteristics in these T center collections. Our results confirm that with only minor optimizations during fabrication, densely populated T centres embedded in silicon can establish a powerful photon-spin interface. This is evidenced by a zero magnetic field zero-field splitting of approximately 140 MHz, electron spin resonance in both bulk and SOI samples under various conditions, and at high magnetic fields near g-max values of~0.033. This study analyzes a stochastic SIR (susceptible, infectious, recovered) epidemic model defined on a social network, where susceptible and infected dynamic interactions follow specific Poisson processes. As the population scale $N$ approaches infinity, we examine the behavior at a critical infection rate scaled as $\lambda_{N} = \lambda/N$. Accurately reconstructing and dense aligning faces in 3D, especially in uncontrolled settings ("in the wild") where images suffer from occlusion or large head movements, remains a difficult challenge due to missing face details and expanded modeling spaces. The core of our approach lies in modeling occlusion and head pose together, which allows us to split a highly complex task into several more tractable subproblems. Consequently, we introduce an end‑to‑end framework called Self-aligned DualFace Regression Network (SADR). First, the Focal Face Keypoint Estimator locates keypoints by selecting well-pose, non-occluded eye regions. Second, the Face Part Aligner and Feature Extractor generates images that are both deposed and split into non-occluded regions via cycles of self-supervised alignment and identity-matching reconstruction. Finally, the Face Parameter Estimator generates a complete model of the head, integrating identity-specific and population-wide characteristics using cycles of self-aligned representation and diverse, pose/occlusion-conditioned matching and merging. Extensive tests on public and private datasets confirm that our technique significantly outperforms existing baseline models.

Donor spins in silicon have already reached benchmark record-breaking coherence times and single-qubit gate fidelities. The subsequent phase of development centers on demonstrating robust two-qubit logic operations, for which the exchange interaction serves as the most favorable coupling mechanism. To facilitate the efficient design of scalable donar-based quantum computers, we simulated the two-electron wave function using full configuration interaction methods integrated with multi-valley effective mass theory. Leveraging our code's high computational efficiency, we examined the exchange interaction, valley occupation probabilities, and electron spatial distributions for pairs of phosphorus donors across diverse lattice positions, orientations, and varying electric field strengths. These results are presented through interactive visualizations that dynamically trace valley and orbital components as donor sites change. Ultimately, our study offers a physically clear and quantitatively precise framework for understanding the positioning and tuning requirements needed to realize high-fidelity two-qubit operations in silicon using donor spins.

Focusing on the field ranges between the first two perpendicular quantum phase transitions—corresponding to the vanishing of the longitudinal conductance at $B_{\perp\;1\;}$ and $B_{\perp\;2\;}$—we observe a distinct diagonal sequence of Hall conductance minima ($S_{\text{H}}$) at intermediate angles rather than the direct connection seen in gapless bulk materials. This discrete diagonal pattern arises from the formation of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-quantized, screw-disclination-like bulk gapless state (mississippi states), situated midway between the edge states dominant at low fields ($E < E_{\parallel\;}\}$) and the typical quantum Hall states dominating other regimes. The resulting filling-factor structure reveals a duality that maps these intermediate perpendicular fields onto an effective out-of-plane field of equal magnitude. Consistently with experiments, our theoretical framework also addresses the sequence of transitions defined by conductance minima along the zero-diagonal trajectory.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmission modes independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of power distribution and resource allocation a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient, decentralized framework that decouples the scheduling and power control processes. The proposed method first distributes power across cells in a decentralized manner and subsequently assigns transmission modes using a non-cooperative game to reach a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. Two different payoff calculation methods within the game model explore the impact of cross-interference representations and the associated communication overhead. Simulation studies in an outdoor, high-density small-scale cellular environment demonstrate that these proposed strategies significantly surpass the performance of static TDD systems.

It also effectively implements the "learning to learn" capability through the use of a more constrained physical framework for the outer loop.

Simultaneously, an improviser agent uses secure rule-based protocols to identify anomalies, retrieve human annotations, apply geometric data augmentation, and continuously improve performance via transfer learning. We tested our method against MNIST and FashionMNIST with intentional corruptions. Results demonstrate improved robustness in both confidence levels and accuracy with only a marginal increase in labeled data compared to our baseline.

K-fold cross-validation is widely adopted for evaluating the effectiveness of machine-learning models and adjusting their hyperparameters. Nevertheless, the inherent random splitting of data increases variability in the training sets across different folds, causing traditional methods to produce more inconsistent results than necessary. Addressing this issue, we have developed Optimized Cross-Validation (OptCV), an technique designed specifically for systematic parameter tuning. In OptCV, key hyperparameters are fixed in advance; consequently, data partitions are de-randomized by anchoring the split based on sorted features—such as temporal ordering in time-series—text document categories like email spam vs. not spam, or the extreme values of any specific feature. We evaluated OptCV across diverse scenarios, including a variety of benchmark tabular datasets, a Google Web Search query analysis, and a real-world Google infrastructure monitoring use case. These studies demonstrated a clear reduction in performance metric variance while maintaining equivalent median performance relative to standard K-fold methods. Developing numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations often requires them to maintain essential features of the continuous solution, such as conservation laws or other geometric attributes. This paper introduces a novel, explicitly time-stepping, multi-step method—constructed as a iterative composition of an explicit one-step rule—that delivers high-order accuracy and approximate conservation. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed approach not only matches the precision of existing methods but also avoids the major limitations associated with current technologies.

Humans are able to handle new tasks by drawing upon and adapting past skills, a process known as generalization. This method builds next-token prediction examples for training and evaluation by arranging tasks in sequence as they appear during test exploration. This simulates the linear journey a learner takes through unseen tasks and allows for the assessment of how the model adapts to each new one. We believe this process will guide multi-task MLMs to focus on identifying task boundaries and connections, thereby improving cross-domain generalization. We test our method on two standard benchmarks and observe a significant performance increase in real-world settings for specific unseen task pairs.

We introduce DISCO, a novel, application-independent framework designed specifically for the generation of counterfactual data. DISCO modularizes existing methods, allowing it to leverage the strengths of current frameworks while providing the benefits of an unified structure and training approach. By creating a common framework, DISCO allows for continuous improvement through updates to individual components without requiring retraining across the board. Furthermore, DISCO introduces a new data structure and specific details essential for generating counterfactual news and images, ensuring consistency. Through extensive experiments on both news generation and image generation tasks using models from different domains, we demonstrated that our model-out of which the news module uses policy gradient methods for specific domain requirements and image module utilizes discrete action frameworks for visual nuances- significantly outperformed baseline approaches in multiple key metrics. Conditional Generative Adverse Networks (cGANs) have demonstrated excellence at class-conditional generation but require multi-label training sets to handle concurrent conditions effectively, where a training sample possesses several tags. Although acquiring this capacity via exhaustive annotation is prohibitively expensive, restricting our scope to individual cases in which additional labels only tag images already marked as positive for existing labels, we can drastically reduce labeling costs. We present a method employing Fast Supervised Label Learning (FSLL) to acquire these labels automatically, proposing that the capacity for a particular tag *t* is computed as one minus the minimum distance between an unlabeled image and any other image sharing that same label. Importantly, if distances are derived from features extracted by a pre-trained deep network such as VGG19, proposed labels are guaranteed high precision. As demonstrated by our experiments conducting personal face attributes addition under five separate indications on the Google Photos dataset, this strategy substantially improves results compared to generating scenarios in which labels do not exist.

The provenances of GeV gamma-rays originating from the jets of radio-emitting galaxies remain unclear. A leading hypothesis suggests these signals arise in accretion flows near the event horizons of supermassive black holes (SMBHs), where jets are anchored. Specifically, this model posits an inverse relationship: higher accretion rates lead to weaker GeV emissions due to a truncated radiation-mediated shock, whereas lower accretion rates produce stronger but jet-suppressed signals from an unmagnetized, advection-dominated accretion flow (AMA). However, recent observations indicate robust GeV gamma-ray output from the IC J3459+00M2 at sub-Eddington accretion rates (~0.001-0.01 of the Eddington limit), situated within jets rather than the accretion flow. Consequently, this study re-examines the mechanisms responsible for IC J3459+00M2's emissions and argues that their origin must be the jet itself, aligning this interpretation with the currently accepted physical properties of Event Horizon Telescope-observed active galactic nuclei.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for identifying cardiac diseases early. However, the automated analysis of heart sounds to detect abnormalities remains challenging due to numerous artifacts and the necessity for extensive data sets for training. To address these issues, we developed 'HeartSound AI,' a comprehensive framework for acquiring, storing, and managing raw auditory data alongside clinical annotations. This system leverages WebAssembly and TensorFlow Lite to facilitate real-time, on-device training and inference on diverse populations of patients. By utilizing transfer learning, the model achieves an F1 score of 0.85 for heart sound classification and effectively detects specific abnormalities, including cardiac murmurs, abnormal S3 and S4 sounds, and prolonged isometric contraction intervals. Additionally, the interface visualizes audios for standard diagnostic methods and provides computed formulations for ischemia assessment. Ultimately, this web-based application promotes accessible, instantaneous, and autonomous analysis of cardiovascular disorders.

Recruiting within large organizations typically requires reviewing a vast pool of applications through interviews, a task that demands both significant effort and complex execution. While recruiting has been a critical business function for decades, most existing approaches to streamlining this workflow—specifically those utilizing machine learning—examine only individual aspects, neglecting the entire recruitment lifecycle. Furthermore, current methods often fail to address the necessary trade-offs among competing optimization criteria. A fundamental hurdle in planning these interview processes lies in managing a massive quantity of potential candidates and intricate applicant data structures. Additionally, the various stages of selection and scheduling compete as conflicting objectives. To address this, we introduce a novel multi-objective and multi-level mathematical modeling framework designed to maximize the use of available information. This model operates across multiple temporal scales and stages, beginning with the identification of efficient stratification strategies for the self-nomination stage submitted by applicants, followed by a unified and coherent model for decision-making and scheduling on a global level. We designed heuristic and exact algorithms capable of generating optimal or near-optimal solutions for the overarching problem. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this holistic approach offers significant advantages over standalone methods focused on individual components.

This study examines various mathematical formulations developed during the current pandemic, which tackle distinct public health issues regarding epidemics and their drivers. We begin by outlining the foundational characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and application to topics such as transmission dynamics and interaction of concurrent viral infections. Our analysis focuses on epidemic curve trajectories, the construction and time-to-event characterization of compartmental models using probability distribution data to fit realistic scenarios—all anchored in the premise that every differential equation system designed for epidemiological tasks must rest upon a robust biological, medical, and contextual rationale derived from its motivating factors. Merely fitting these mathematical equations to available data without ensuring biological plausibility may yield statistical validity; yet, without a firm understanding of the biological underpinnings, these models offer minimal utility for the effective management, mitigation, or ultimate containment of the SARS-CoV-2 outbreak.

This theoretical study explores various facets of the dynamic atom-molecule conversion occurring within spin-1 Bose–Einstein condensates. Specifically, we analyze the mechanism by which, under tailored dark-state conditions, the coupling between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the robust formation of atomic-molecular dyads from three initial zero-spin atoms, involving two photons and one molecule containing two photons. Additionally, the research employs stochastic simulation methods to investigate the fundamental limits of molecule production under realistic experimental scenarios, confirming a significant formation of molecule. The analysis provides detailed insights into the underlying physical processes, notably through the examination of distinct dynamic regimes. Furthermore, the study addresses specific challenges associated with photodissociation, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding and optimizing this atom-to-molecule transition process.

We introduce a new and adaptable DNA-storage architecture that establishes hierarchical structures among files sharing the same primer pair to facilitate data updates. While previous approaches treated a 20-base PCR primer pair as a single discrete object, our model defines it instead as an autnominantly managed storage partition equipped with its unique indexing structure. We note that although mutually compatible primed are naturally limited in quantity, the internal address space within each partition is effectively expansive. By exploiting this flexibility, we realize advanced storage semantics, including logical hierarchies and robust update mechanisms. Furthermore, building on the natural characteristics of PCR prefix-matching, we devised a method for converting arbitrary indexing protocols into PCR-variants. This approach reuses variable primed extensions, targeting specific index segments to precisely locate particular objects (such as specific files or folders) within the partition. Empirical wet-lab testing underscores this proposal's feasibility, highlighting a 140-fold decrease in sequencing expenses when retrieving smaller components from a stored partition.

Accurately and quickly predicting river flow velocities is critical for various applications, such as managing flood risks; however, traditional shallow water equations (SWE) solvers are computationally demanding, often necessitating detailed, high-resolution bathymetry data. This research introduces a two-stage framework that leverages machine learning for rapid SWE simulation, designed to function with coarse-grained bottom data. The approach first trains a learning-based solver to map velocity fields from initial and boundary conditions directly to the solution. Subsequently, specific river characteristics—derived from Stochastic Generalized Utilities (SGU)—are integrated as inputs to drive the solver, enabling it to predict flows in various water bodies without retraining on specific domain details. Tests using field measurements from the Rhine and synthetic datasets demonstrate high fidelity in capturing both local flow dynamics and broader spatial patterns. Success in these trials suggests that the proposed method could significantly assist in monitoring and overseeing diverse river systems.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels, allowing devices like smartphones with limited internal dynamic ranges to capture full brightness and contrast. This study proposes a technique to automatically determine exposure parameters using a camera characteristic function. Additionally, it defines a novel merging approach relying on weighted averaging through an optimization framework. These strategies have been deployed as an HDR application for mobile use, proving their practical application. Comparative analyses against existing benchmarks confirm the method's efficiency and computational effectiveness.

This study presents a performance evaluation comparing Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners for cardiac mechanical simulations on both structured and unstructured finite element meshes. Since myocardial mechanical behavior follows three-dimensional finite elasticity equations—which are discretized spatially to form a massive nonlinear algebraic system solved via the Newton-Krylov method—this framework relies on BDDC and AMG acceleration techniques to resolve the associated Jacobian systems. A thorough analysis of critical BDDC settings ensures an equitable comparison. Key focuses include assessing the effectiveness of various direct solvers within the local and coarse problems of the algorithm, investigating the consequences of different choices for BDDC primal degrees of freedom, and evaluating how finite element degree influences performance. Scalability experiments were conducted across large-scale systems spanning up to 2,222 domains, encompassing more than 15,000 elements. Crucially, this effort involved extensive Frank-Hertz cycle simulations involving over 15,000 nodes per system. Additional findings address the implications of specific experimental configurations, including electrical conduction-my mechanical coupling mechanisms and software implementation details utilizing the Trilinos software library.

Standard diffusive expansion is typified by a Gaussian distribution where the mean square displacement scales linearly against time, yet this standard behavior fails when correlations or heterogeneity arise. Consequently, this study analyzes the diffusion of fractional (long-time memory-corrupted), Brownian walkers under conditions of varying and spatially non-uniform diffusivity. The primary goal involves translating these microscopic, individual attributes visible as population-scale temporal evolution into physical insights regarding the broader context of self-similar diffusion. Furthermore, the work evaluates the viability of linking such features across various self-similar diffusion regimes, detailing both the potential and inherent constraints. Results are structured within a unified framework applied here to classic phenomena, including linear and nonlinear Laplace diffusive systems, along with their respective variations.

We examine the interplay between linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity within a pair of optical resonators. By investigating both numerical simulations and analytical methods, we identify that this specific combination can produce either distinct phases of operation or surprising transient behaviors. We further quantify the competing relationships involving coupling types, nonlinear effects, and scattering to determine critical thresholds. At these thresholds, unbounded frequency shifts lead to complex, time-dependent behaviors in the system.

This study introduces a deep learning framework that utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from very low-resolution data across various Reynolds numbers. The Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) serves as the model for reconstruction and is assessed using direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent channel flows with large longitudinal ribs tested at multiple Reynolds numbers. The findings indicate the model's capability to accurately generate high-resolution velocity fields, encompassing both field properties and turbulent statistics, from inputs derived from two distinct low-resolution resolutions. Furthermore, the results demonstrate the model's potential for supergeneralization by reconstructing velocity fields at Reynolds levels different from those used during training, without additional instruction or adaptation for those specific cases, effectively handling unseen scenarios in its scope.

Although significant advancements have been made in applying reinforcement learning to robotics, gaming, and other demanding areas, considerable obstacles persist when deploying these algorithms in critical, evolving open-world settings. A primary issue remains the tendency of reinforcement learning models to generalize poorly to new tasks lying outside their training data distributions; consequently, continual learning algorithms have garnered considerable attention. Beyond developing such algorithmic methods, there is an urgent need for structured challenge environments, tailored experiments, and evaluation metrics analogous to those established in benchmarking frameworks like Atari. We argue that current open-world REAL-world datasets are insufficient and propose the creation of a dedicated continuous learning evaluation protocol. To support this, we have devised a dataset initialization and evaluation framework suitable for realistic domains, which we have implemented using office automation robots. Additionally, we have evaluated it with a benchmarking suite that includes both existing and newly developed experiments, proving its utility. This protocol is designed to be generalizable, with the potential for replication and future proofing across other robotics systems. Thus, this approach offers a pathway to establish a rigorous open-world continuous learning evaluation standard in the robotics community.

Process discovery encompasses a range of methods designed to understand operational workflows directly from their data traces. However, since workflows inherently evolve, any corresponding models must also be updated regularly; failure to adapt risks resulting in models that inaccurately reflect the underlying processes. To verify if such models require updates, we introduced a framework for identifying process changes by mapping difference diagrams between discovery outcomes obtained from current event logs against those from discovery results using historical logs. We present the three components of our approach: constructing a bridge between event logs and these difference diagrams; utilizing event-level tags to inject domain knowledge into the visualization; and employing a satisfaction survey mechanism to incorporate feedback from process experts on those enriched diagrams. This holistic methodology allows business process managers to integrate knowledge from both historical and current event logs when validating discovered models, thereby significantly enhancing result accuracy. To demonstrate this approach's applicability and effectiveness, we applied the methodology to a case study.

This research explores cross-lingual sentiment analysis for Croatian news through zero- and few-shot learning approaches. The study focuses on categorizing Croatian news into positive, negative, and neutral classes by leveraging the Slovene dataset. The methodology employs an architecture built on a trilingual BERT model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian texts. The paper examines various configurations using bilingual datasets, introducing a simple multitask model designed for sentiment classification, and assesses performance under both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios via single- and multitask comparisons in Slovene and Croatian.

X-ray imaging likely harbors complex yet predictifiable traits that indicate COVID-19 severity, potentially enabling the practical deployment of affordable diagnostics for prioritizing scarce resources for affected individuals, despite prior efforts failing to explain the basis of such predictions using automated analysis methods. This study aims to fill that gap by investigating the explainable material cues within pulmonary X-rays associated with severe status in COVID-19 patients through a novel framework. It utilizes state-of-the-art, multidimensional image characteristics captured via deep convolutional neural networks, explaining their relevance through a subtractive lattice model for concepts. Evaluations across extensive, diverse datasets demonstrate that this approach not only achieves highly accurate prediction of whether a patient is severe or not with a focus toward rare positive instances, but also reveals distinct phenotypic concepts usable for understanding why an individual receives a severe or non-severe classification. These findings were verified through rigorous cross-validation strategies and independently on external data sources.

This study utilizes detailed observations in both sub-millimeter and millimeter wavelengths to examine the oblateness and star formation rates within the massive, star-forming "4c 3341" galaxy. Our findings indicate that 4c 3341 possesses a stellar ellipsicity ($e_\text{star}$) of approximately 0.33, classifying it as significantly steeper than peer galaxies on both sides of its mid-infrared color axis, which lies near equilibrium oblateness values of 0.17–0.21. This discrepancy is particularly evident at similar faces-on sizes ($D_\text{f})$, where the galaxy displays formal specific star formation rates ($sfr_\text{spat}$)$ that appear under-active by roughly 0.33. The formation of such pronounced disk tilts, alongside associated gas dynamical stresses, creates an environment conducive to the suppression of star formation. Our results suggest that the combined development of leaner disks and diminished star formation constitutes a feedback mechanism responsible for producing ultra-massive galaxies.

This paper outlines the initial observations and uses a quantitative approach to estimate the energies, directions, and origins of two specific SNDPs. This study utilizes 13 CO and CN thermal emission spectra from the low-mass giant star 20 Scuti to estimate its atmospheric radial temperature profile. When compared to the spectral type's anticipated effective temperature, the measured spectrum exhibits a discrepancy that implies suppressed atmospheric convection. Furthermore, when contrasted with stellar modeling, the data indicates an inverted atmospheric semi-vertical gradient characterized by effective temperatures that increase toward the star's surface. These findings collectively point to an intermediate-timescale atmospheric process—intermediate in timescale between surface convection and global tidal Qy mechanisms—that induces atmospheric expansion in 20 Scuti. Such process may similarly operate on other giant stars possessing relatively rapid rotation rates, perhaps resulting in measurable impacts upon surface rotational dynamics. The analysis concludes by suggesting further causes or implications of the detected rotational discrepancies, particularly regarding the separation between surface and core rotation rates.

Rapidly circulating through social media on a global scale, fake news threatens users and entire communities, especially as it emerges with alarming speed. While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where accumulating large, well-annotated datasets is impractical. Furthermore, integrating knowledge about new events currently necessitates retraining models or continuous fine-tuning—a process that is often costly, inefficient, and unfeasible in real-world applications.

To solve these issues, this paper introduces MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework capable of learning to identify fake news from newly emerged events using limited verified data (few-shot setting). The solution employs a dual-level meta-learning strategy: at the sample level, it optimizes a classification model for specific new events via feedback from social media interactions; concurrently, at the parameter level, it maintains generalized metadata capabilities to recognize and adapt to future emerging events. Empirical tests across three data sets confirm the significant success of our proposed approach.

Quantum tunneling, a process without classical correspondence that can compete with Coulomb interactions to generate complex behavior, serves as a focal topic. Silicon doped with phosphorus allows researchers to position atoms with precision and investigate the regimes resulting from this competition. However, current systems rely on wavefunctions tied to crystal band symmetries, creating inherent sensitivity to tunneling effects. This study employs scanning tunneling microscopy to directly visualize lattice-aperiodic interference patterns formed by the conduction band minima in silicon. These observations confirm a strong correlation between interference characteristics and crystal orientation relative to the dopant arrangement. Additionally, the work quantifies tunneling-induced shifts in quantum points near the metastable stability limit for hyperstable traps, or, with sufficient external fields, creates dopant-free interference zones that exhibit the desired nonlinearity-required phase transitions. Furthermore, the authors establish a new method using external flux to switch between quantum states, effectively swapping the dominant interaction type, and demonstrate that this conversion remains feasible even when wavefunctions are confined to valence bands where Coulomb forces prevail.

Complex systems often consist of interacting components governed by simple, universal principles. Granh neural networks (GNNs) offer a beneficial inductive bias related to such systems; however, research into generalizing to novel system instances remains underdeveloped. We addressed this by training GNNs to model time-series data from hypothetical electric circuits, equipping the models with both topological knowledge (structure) and dynamical knowledge (interaction dynamics). Within an optimized framework employing a gradient-based loss function, we specifically focused on GNNs trained with known graph architecture. Results indicate that such models can model an infinite number of circuit configurations using a single training set for a specific subset, effectively serving both to forecast individual node outputs and rank the overall stability of different circuit configurations. We further analyzed various types of learned parameters regarding their capacity to model different nonlinear functions of the inputs. This study highlights the potential of GNNs with structured input Topology for modeling time-series from systems with explicit structural definitions, with significant implications for applications in physics and material science.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive technique for ablating intracranial structures, with segmentation of pre-and post-operative MR images playing a crucial role in planning and evaluating the procedure. Although existing methods for estimating these structures from T1- and contrast-enhanced (CE) MPRAGE images achieve high accuracy, there remains a gap in automated systems specifically designed for T1-weighted (non-contrast) images. These systems are essential in clinical environments, particularly given the increasing prevalence of T1 sequences due to multi-sequence MRI acquisitions often automated during radiological workflows. To address this need, we introduce an end-to-end convolutional neural network that simultaneously maps substructures of the healthy infant brain and predicts CE image intensity values based on the segmented components. Evaluations conducted on 200 infant brains demonstrated that external testing achieved an average infant brain segmentation Dice coefficient of 0.82 alongside reconstruction errors of 0.82 for CE images, underscoring the utility of proposed approaches in automating the analysis of intracranial pediatric lesions such as LITT.

Feature extraction offers a viable solution to dimensionality reduction, a challenge faced across various fields, yet inherent limitations often constrain traditional methods. To address this, we introduce a novel framework leveraging contrastive learning, currently a prominent area of research, to enhance the extraction process. First, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is employed as the initial extractor to generate features that facilitate subsequent contrastive training without requiring labeled information. Second, a contrastive autoencoder refines these features through unsupervised learning to maximize separation between positive and negative samples in the latent space, thereby improving representation quality. We validate the proposed method's effectiveness on several high-dimensional datasets and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Model selection or sparse modelling for categorical variables remains problematic, even with a moderate variable count, as encoding each category requires a parameter, quickly leading to non-solutions. Although Group Lasso is an established and efficient tool for selecting continuous or categorical variables, its estimates for individual levels of selected factors are rarely identical. Because of the lack uniformity, resulting models often fail to achieve true sparsity, hindering interpretability. We address this by proposing a two-stage strategy: initially, dimensionality is reduced using Group Lasso; subsequently, final selection is made over a narrowed candidate space via an information criterion applied to clusters of factor levels constructed after the initial selection phase. We examine algorithm accuracy within sparse, high-dimensional contexts, applying our approach to both synthetic examples and realistic datasets, demonstrating that our methods generally outperform current-state-of-the-art algorithms regarding prediction accuracy or model size efficiency at the variable dimension.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit human-like capabilities across many natural language tasks, it has remained largely unexamined whether their ability to internalize knowledge from structured formats like Knowledge Graphs (KGS)—which encode semantic relationships between real-world entities—offers advantages over equivalent formulations in natural language sentences. Addressing this inquiry, we fine-tuned the TRL-based ChatGPT-3.5-l337 model on a dataset comprising the Wikidata Knowledge Graph (WikDS), alongside parallel sentence descriptions of those graph entries. Subsequent evaluations reveal that the model trained on knowledge graph data outperforms the one trained on sentences in both factual and instructional response metrics, specifically regarding the accuracy of generated information and instruction following. Moreover, we observe improved cost-effectiveness and reduced response lengths from the dataset tailored to knowledge graphs. Further analyses suggest these results stem from a more rigorous emphasis on data accuracy and an optimized presentation of crucial details due to the knowledge graph structure. Finally, we analyze the potential pitfalls associated with this approach and offer suggestions for future research.

Experiments conducted over a year demonstrate that this solution significantly enhances visual quality and stabilizes rendering by frame, while maintaining minimal overhead compared to existing techniques.

Our investigation focuses on the criteria required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. We determine that creating genuine multipartite entanglement is unattainable if the interaction cavity of an initially uncorrelated atom shares only classical correlations with any other cavity. The Jost function method has been adapted within the RPA framework to detect poles in the complex energy plane exhibiting complex RPA eigenvalues. This approach successfully identified poles associated with RPA excited states, specifically locating the electric dipole giants resonances in $^{16}$O. Despite the conventional view of the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O as a single state with significant strength and width, the results indicate that, under RPA conditions, the resonance comprises multiple poles. Each pole functions as a separate entity with distinctive widths, underlying origins, response characteristics regarding residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures.

Community detection poses significant challenges yet remains highly relevant across diverse fields, encompassing everything from power grids and atmospheric science to social networks and financial markets. However, in many of these domains—such as power grids and financial markets—the dynamic nature of the data is critical; therefore, this work concentrates on clustering dynamic systems. We introduce a framework designed to cluster differential equations by employing a discrete approximation of the solution manifold, where each region within this grid shares an associated vector field. By integrating these loops in the gridded phase space, we derive a discrete state-transition model, where each community corresponds to a loop. We determine the optimal partitioning of the phase space into these loops and calculate their parameters in a manner odds to model learning in physical systems, allowing for efficient prediction and the capacity to generalize to unobserved trajectories. Finally, we demonstrate this method's applicability by applying it to multiple systems of differential equations.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly with either inaccurate gradient estimates or poor-quality sentence embeddings. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN to feed sparse, semantically meaningful sentence representations to the discriminator. This is achieved by treating the embedding matrix as an over-complete dictionary, approximating generator output features at each timestep through a linear combination of only a few selected word embeddings. These robust semantic representations streamline adversarial learning and ensure full differentiability, while empirical results across multiple datasets demonstrate performance gains, particularly improving BLEU scores for whole sequences.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. Our results indicate that the statistical pair distribution of inhabited planetary systems can effectively detect interstellar transfer of life under the specific condition that ejecta move with sufficient divergence relative to stellar motions. By offering heuristic estimates of key parameters in different astrophysical contexts, we conclude that open and globular clusters are the most suitable regions for testing this hypothesis.

A core focus of animal populations research is understanding how space is used and how resources are selected, a topic often addressed through telemetry data and resource selection functions (RSF). Wildlife research also heavily emphasizes estimating and modeling population density and size; recent advancements in spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models facilitate this by analyzing individual encounter histories alongside auxiliary capture location data. While SCR models contain encounter probability functions that resemble RSFs, there was historically a gap in extending these models for explicit joint inference on space use and resource selection. We introduce a statistical framework for these objectives that merges SCR data—such as that generated by mist-nets, trap-catch, or camera traps—with spatial resource usage data from telemetry-tagged individuals utilizing marginal likelihood methods to simultaneously estimate SCR and RSF model parameters. Our methodology demonstrates increased precision for estimating both population density and the parameters of standard SCR models. Furthermore, we identify that while SCR data can sufficiently estimate RSF parameters for analyzing space usage, accuracy improves significantly when telemetry data are integrated. Critically, we find that conventional SCR models using symmetric, stationary encounter probability functions tend to yield density bias when space use varies with landscape characteristics. Consequently, when estimating density using capture-recapture, it is essential to account for spatial usage patterns wherever feasible.

Multilayer networks represent a valuable tool for modeling and analyzing the dynamical properties of diverse systems. While providing a more realistic depiction with richer complexity compared to single-layer models, they inherently introduce analytical difficulties. This work presents an approach to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by constructing an "inverted" join of matrices associated with both inter and intralayer interaction topologies. This yields a unified framework for dynamics that allows predictions and generalizations from single-layer systems to apply directly to the multi-layer context. We verify these methods using mathematical proofs, analytical techniques, and numerical simulations across various multi-layer structural designs. Ultimately, we define criteria for when a layer specific dynamic behavior emerges exclusively within the combined multilayer system.
